summary: At just 1.6 square miles, Keyes packs over 5,300 residents into a density that rivals some inner-ring suburbs of much larger cities — yet it sits squarely on the flat, open agricultural floor of the San Joaquin Valley, surrounded by almond orchards and dairy operations rather than strip malls and office parks. The setting delivers huge unobstructed skies and reliable sunshine — averaging 9.5 hours of daylight illumination per day — but summer highs push well into the 90s and beyond, making shade and air conditioning non-negotiable from June through September. Keyes functions as a bedroom community tethered to nearby Modesto and the broader Highway 99 corridor; there is no major employment center within the town itself, and the surrounding economy runs on agriculture, food processing, and logistics. A median home value of $335,500 against a median household income of roughly $59,300 yields a price-to-income ratio near 5.7, meaning a conventional mortgage would consume a steep share of a typical household's gross earnings, while rents averaging $1,361 take about 27.5% of that same median income — tight but closer to conventional affordability thresholds. The poverty rate of 27.5% underscores that many households operate with thin margins. Keyes is, at its core, a small, flat, sun-drenched Central Valley settlement where affordable housing prices by California standards come bundled with long commutes and limited local amenities.
